overview: This Orissa record spans later Eastern Ganga rule, the expansion of the Gajapati kingdom, and subsequent regional and imperial governments in Odisha. Puri’s Jagannath temple helped rulers express their authority. The atlas dates, 1279 to 1650, are coverage limits rather than one dynasty’s lifetime. Its coarse western outline actually omits Cuttack, Puri and Konark, important centres discussed here; it should not be read as their kingdom’s complete boundary.

periods.title: Later Eastern Ganga rule
periods.summary: The record begins within an established dynasty. Kapilendra replaces the Eastern Ganga ruling line in 1435.

periods.title: Gajapatis and successor rulers
periods.summary: Kapilendra’s expansion is followed by later rulers and dynastic changes. Mukunda’s death and Afghan conquest in 1568 end this independent royal phase.

periods.title: Afghan power and Khurda
periods.summary: Afghan rule follows conquest, while a smaller Bhoi kingdom at Khurda restores a local centre of royal and temple authority.

periods.title: Mughal administration and regional continuity
periods.summary: Mughal government reorganizes revenue districts. Local institutions continue beyond the atlas cutoff of 1650.

items.text: Kapilendra took power in 1435, replacing the Eastern Ganga ruling line. He initially faced resistance from local chiefs as well as neighbouring powers. His kingdom had to be built through political struggle: a coronation did not automatically make every regional lord obedient.

A Telugu inscription at a Warangal gateway records the capture of the fort by Ambira-deva, also known as Hamvira, a son of Kapilendra. Its date corresponds to 2 February 1460. This surviving local record gives a concrete foothold for Gajapati expansion into Telangana, far beyond the Odisha coast.

An inscription at Puri records Kapilendra remitting taxes on salt and cowries in favour of the god Purushottama. Revenue and religion met in a written royal order. This was a specified temple concession, rather than evidence that everyone in the kingdom stopped paying those taxes.

Another Puri inscription records the king giving a sari cloth called Pundarika gopa to Jagannath. The order passed through a named storekeeper and superintendent. Even a royal religious gift needed someone to receive instructions and look after the goods.

Sarala Dasa’s fifteenth-century Odia Mahabharata brought the epic into an Odia literary world. In historian Pravakar Sethi’s reading, its food descriptions include boiled rice, pulses, vegetables, milk sweets and occasional plantain-leaf plates. These are glimpses through literature, whose surviving versions vary, rather than a menu proven for every family.

Sethi also describes wedding scenes in Sarala’s work: relatives arrive at the bride’s home, roads are cleaned, walls decorated, and young women collect water from seven houses for the couple’s ritual bath. A wedding could become a neighbourhood project. The detail belongs to the literary account, not a rule for every community.

A 1291 inscription at Simhachalam records an endowment supporting teachers of Vedic texts, grammar, poetry and drama. It belongs to the Eastern Ganga world inherited by later rulers. A temple could support demanding study as well as worship, although this example tells us about a particular learned institution.

The scholar Divakara’s Laksanadarsa retells the Pandavas’ story while illustrating grammatical points in its sections. Adventure and grammar could share the same page. Subrahmanyam discusses it among the literature associated with Prataparudra’s learned world.

A short Sanskrit drama, Parasurama Vijaya, is attributed to Kapilendra. The work indicates that it was performed during a festival at the Jagannath temple before 1458. Courtly literature could be heard and watched by an audience, rather than remaining only in a manuscript.

sections.title: Giant wheels and objects from a palace

items.text: The Sun Temple at Konark was already standing before this map record begins. Built under Narasimha Deva I in the thirteenth century, it presents the sun god’s chariot through monumental stone architecture. Its 24 carved wheels are about three metres across: a wheel taller than many adults, with no chance of fitting on a bicycle.

Konark’s sculptors carved musicians, dancers and scenes of social life into the temple. Its surviving dance hall and audience hall help show how architecture, performance and worship belonged together. Stone preserves gestures and instruments that would otherwise vanish when the music stopped.

At Barabati Fort in Cuttack, excavators identified a large pillared hall and adjoining courtyard in the fifteenth- and sixteenth-century phase. The hall’s surviving width is about twenty metres. Its foundations offer firmer evidence for royal space than the conflicting later stories about a many-storeyed palace.

Debris filling that hall included Chinese porcelain dated around the sixteenth century, coloured lime plaster and small beads shaped like areca nuts. The fragments bring imported objects and bright decoration into an otherwise ruined room. A broken plate can preserve evidence of a connection much farther away than the palace walls.

A sculpture recovered from Barabati’s moat shows a couple on a swing. Archaeologists assigned it stylistically to the Gajapati period and suggested it may have decorated a temple. Its playful subject survives, although the displaced carving cannot tell us the names or everyday routines of a real family.

sections.title: A written Saturday and a changing kingdom

items.text: The 1460 Warangal inscription supplies a tiny language sample: Vadda-varamu, meaning “Saturday.” This is the editor’s Roman-letter rendering of a word in a Telugu inscription, not an image of its original letters. It formed part of the date recording a military capture. The kingdom’s surviving records therefore include languages used beyond its Odia-speaking core.

After the 1568 conquest, Ramachandra Deva of the Bhoi line established a smaller kingdom at Khurda and restored Jagannath worship at Puri. Successive rulers retained a role supervising the temple. Political authority had contracted, but royal ritual and local institutions continued.

Under Mughal administration from 1592, Odisha’s revenue organization included the districts of Jaleswar, Bhadrak and Kataka, with Puri in Kataka. Collecting and organizing revenue became part of an imperial framework. The atlas’s final date of 1650 does not mark the disappearance of Odisha’s towns, languages or communities.

ending.text: The large independent kingdom was broken by dynastic struggles and the Afghan conquest of 1568. Smaller Khurda and continuing temple institutions survived; Mughal administration followed in 1592. The imported 1650 endpoint is a map cutoff, not the end of Odisha’s people or regional identity.
